We conducted interviews with grantee partners who had faced reprisals as well as experts in this area to develop a report on types of reprisals faced as well as peer to peer advice from activists and recommendations for policy makers and funders.1) Reprisals initiative: In response to increasing repressive governments and contexts due to expanding authoritarianism and anti-rights movement that pose more threats to civic space and WHRDs and structurally excluded activists and community members, UAF FA partnered and strengthened partnerships with 15 grantee partners and 9 practitioners across 10 countries who contributed to research and documentation of their experiences and resources on reprisals. This deepened UAF FA's understanding of contexts along with the types of reprisals and presence of resources and infrastructure (or lack of resources and infrastructure needed) to support WHRDs, WROs and feminist movements as they face retribution for their human rights activism. UAF FA is building out a microsite that provides resources for WHRDs, WROs and feminist activists who face reprisals to help plan, manage and partner with others. We are also conducting a social media campaign to highlight these issues. UAF FA will continue to partner with our grantees, advisors and participants who contributed to the report via advocacy opportunities, grant support and networking connections. 2) Alliance for Sustainable Feminist Movements: These global advocacy opportunities and spaces strengthened partnerships between UAF FA and members in the Alliance for Sustainable Feminist Movements by creating shared political agendas. 3) Spotlight Civil Society Global Reference Group: This engagement with these actors improved our partnerships in advancing advocacy for more funding and better practices supporting feminist movements.

1) SRI. 1 collective of sex worker-led movement showed up as a delegation at the UNHRC and other global advocacy spaces to advocate for their rights and shift harmful narratives. They successfully partnered with other allies to make a strong case in support for sex workers' rights. 2) NSWP. A sex worker collective, including five trans and queer sex worker, participated and spoke on different panels addressing sex workers rights, trans liberation, mutual aid, and philanthropy. These events were co-hosted with other allies, including CMI, showcasing partnerships and solidarity across feminist movements. These opportunities increased advocacy, collective messaging and resistance, and visibility due to their participation. 3) BPPP. 1 sex worker collective and their delegates showed their shared political messaging that successfully challenged and pushed back against harmful narratives conveyed and published by the Special Rapporteur on Violence Against Women (SP VAW). They gained partnerships with other feminist allies to share the message that sex workers and the trans community should not be erased and excluded from these spaces. Sex worker organizations and advocates gained more knowledge and experience navigating this space and the UN system. 1) With CMI continued long-term grant support, a global women's rights coalition (WHRDIC) now has a strategic framework as well as a structure and governance structure with clear working groups delineations, decision-making process, and more to support its long term sustenance. 2) At HRC59, a delegation of 22 sex workers were able to hold their own event, provide oral statements, and advocate for bodily autonomy and rights of sex workers and combat right wing narratives that weaponize women’s safety to target and demonize trans people. 3) With CMI support, a youth queer, black, indigenous, people of color-led (BIPOC) grassroots collective held a festival during CSW, and provided a space for activists to rest, connect, and engage in healing-centered activities through art, storytelling, and movement-building. They facilitated care spaces, including mental health workshops and joy and grief circles, throughout CSW to offer activists emotional support, peer connection, and moments of respite from high-intensity advocacy.1) With CMI's continued long-term grant support, a global women's rights coalition (WHRDIC) now has a strategic framework as well as a structure and governance structure with clear working group delineations, decision-making process, and more to support its long-term sustenance. This resulted in the establishment of working groups that created spaces and opportunities for joint trainings, strategizing, campaigning, and advocacy that collectivized voices of WHRDs and feminist activists from different contexts. Their work strengthened collective mobilization, advocacy, and representation of lived experiences that informed the advocacy agenda in key global spaces such as CSW and Geneva UNHRC, and campaigns addressing WHRDs violations and unjust cases, the violence, and genocide in Sudan and Palestine, and reproductive rights. 2) At HRC59, a delegation of 22 sex workers was able to hold their own event, provide oral statements, and advocate for bodily autonomy and rights of sex workers and combat right-wing narratives that weaponize women’s safety to target and demonize trans people. This resulted in strengthened leadership and advocacy skills to navigate UN spaces as well as incorporate learnings to take back to their organizations and home countries to enhance their advocacy, deepened relationships through high-level bilateral meetings with states, and secured Special Rapporteur support for a joint UN report on sex work, poverty, and health — a major opportunity to influence global human rights standards. 3) With CMI support, a youth queer, black, indigenous, people of color-led (BIPOC) grassroots collective held a festival during CSW and provided a space for activists to rest, connect, and engage in healing-centered activities through art, storytelling, and movement-building. They facilitated care spaces, including mental health workshops and joy and grief circles, throughout CSW to offer activists emotional support, peer connection, and moments of respite from high-intensity advocacy. This resulted in strengthened and deepened relationships with youths in different regions, and improved management of emotional stress and burnout in these fast-paced global advocacy spaces. These actions allowed youths to have a safe space to gather, rest, collect themselves, bond, and energize them to engage in advocacy actions and provide input at CSW69 (plus now preparing for CSW70 post-grant period) and with the High-Level Policy Forum by providing input on youth-and community-centered approaches to inform multilateral spaces that shape global norms and priorities.

1) SRI. With CMI funding, a delegation of sex workers from Sexual Rights Initiative (SRI) and Global Network of Sex Work Projects (NSWP) from many countries across different regions were supported to engage at the 56th Session of the UN Human Rights Council (UNHRC) in Geneva in June and October 2024. The result of advocacy engagement in these spaces strengthened collaboration with allies and increased their visibility and messaging/advocacy. This included working closely with organisations like Amnesty International, WO=MEN, MamaCash, and others, the delegation bolstered its messaging through joint programming, including side events and strategic discussions. The side event "Decriminalising Sex Work: A Human Rights Imperative" was well attended and a question about the side event was even posed to the Special Rapporteur on violence against women (SP VAW) during a press conference organised by the mandate holder to launch her report. The communications campaign played a crucial role in raising awareness of sex workers’rights and challenging harmful narratives and ideas. The high level of engagement across multiple platforms helped to disseminate the delegation’s key messages widely, reaching stakeholders across different sectors and reinforcing the call for decriminalisation. These advocacy spaces and the opportunity to speak out against the harmful narratives and ideas from the report put out by the SP on VAW. 2) NWSP. With CMI support, a sex worker collective and five activists participated through advocacy at CSW 69 & Beijing +30 review events. These actions resulted in increased visbility and amplification with heads of states, policymakers and other feminist activists countering harmful narratives and defending their rights. Additionally, an impromptu but strategic protest outside the French embassy that was discussing work in the porn industry and the Nordic model, but sidelined and excluded sex workers who are impacted from these discussions, raised visibility about sex workers' attendance, participation and resistance to the Nordic model. The collective also supported 5 trans and queer sex worker activists to attend and speak on different pannels at official side and NGO CSW & B+30 review events. These panels were co-hosted with other feminist coalitions, including AWID, CMI, ILGA, SRI, and Wo=Men, thus highlighting deep solidarity and partnerships across feminist groups. 3) BPPP. 1 collective of sex workers and trans activists was supported to attend and engage in advocacy at the UNHCR 56th session in Geneva to defend and promote sex workers' rights, along with contributing to an alternative framing and narrative around sex work. ex worker organizations and advocates gained more knowledge and experience navigating this space and the UN system. 1) Continued long-term CMI support and investment WHRDIC is strengthened with new governance structure, strategic framework, clear working groups, decision-making processes that contribute to its longer-term sustainability and ability to be more resilient to defend and advance WHRD's rights. 2) Deep investment and support from CMI contributed to stronger sex worker-led advocacy and alliance-building to defend their own rights and space at global advocacy UN spaces. 3) A queer, BIPOC, youth-led activist network created and facilitated healing and collective care spaces that supported rest, connection, engagement with healing activities, including mental health workshops, that supported emotional suppport, peer connection and respite during the high-intensity advocacy activities at CSW. Three grantees reported creating and/or defending 8 spaces for activists to participate in advocacy. I) A queer, BIPOC, youth-led activist network created and facilitated online consultations with youth across many regions, as well as collective care spaces that supported rest, connection, and engagement with healing activities during the high-intensity advocacy activities at CSW and the High-Level Political Forum. This resulted in deepened connections with youths across different regions and active engagement in providing input into youth-centered policies in two global spaces during 1) CSW69 and preparations for CSW70, as well as the 2) High-Level Political Forum (that was not part of their original plan). II) A global women's rights coalition (WHRDIC) created opportunities in four global advocacy spaces through various working groups. 1) The Advocacy working group organized, conducted advocacy training and joint advocacy for 25 WHRDs in Geneva during WHRD Advocacy weeks from 2024-2025. 2) Another global advocacy space included CSW69 where the Coalition provided a safe space for activists to organize and advocate with state delegates and ambassadors. 3) The Coalition contributed to advocacy for the 4th International Conference on Financing for Development and mapped the effects of funding cuts as evidence for advocacy-building. 4) With the Coalition for the International Criminal Court (ICC), WHRDIC co-authored Guidelines for WHRDs attending the Special Session of the Assembly of State Parties (ASP) with members and the Coalition for the ICC. III) 2 reported examples at the global and national levels. 1) Strengthened leadership and advocacy capacity of sex workers, most of whom engaged with the UN for the first time and who reported major increases in their confidence and skills. Many of the delegates have followed-up with the UN mechanisms upon their return. One of the delegates from Guyana who was supported by the grant said the experience “exceeded expectations” and that being able to speak on behalf of Caribbean sex workers was “amazing” because they are rarely represented at the UN. Delegates brought back strategies and information that will directly strengthen their organisations’ national advocacy. Another delegate from Mozambique shared that she would use lessons from Geneva in her upcoming meeting with judges in Mozambique, ensuring her organisation can better engage with national justice institutions. 2) Secured Special Rapporteur support for a joint UN report on sex work, poverty, and health that was a major opportunity to influence global human rights standards.

Secured Special Rapporteur support for a joint UN report on sex work, poverty, and health that was a major opportunity to influence global human rights standards. The grantee reported, "An exciting example is the delegation’s meeting with Professor Olivier De Schutter, the UN Special Rapporteur on Extreme Poverty and Human Rights, where delegates proposed that his mandate collaborate with the Dr Tlaleng Mofokeng, the UN Special Rapporteur on Health to produce a joint report on sex work, poverty, and health. During this meeting, sex worker delegates shared evidence about economic precarity, lack of social protection, and the health impacts of criminalisation. Professor De Schutter responded very positively and indicated that the joint report could move forward as soon as the delegation submitted their documentation. This demonstrates that the grant directly enabled the delegation to: present sex worker-led analysis to influential UN mandates; counter harmful narratives by viewing the impacts of criminalisation and other legal regimes impact on sex workers right to health and a life free from poverty; build strategic relationships with both Special Rapporteurs; and secure a major follow-up advocacy outcome that can shape global human rights standards."Grantees did not report on any achievements under this outcome. This is due to a more hostile geopolitical environment, including the rise of anti-gender ideology and regressive policies, which make it more challenging and conducive for the passage of laws or policies. Additionally, grantees supported have been in the process of engaging in restructuring and strengthening their organizational structures and capacities; deepening their partnerships to collectivize diverse voices to build a shared political agenda; building out care and respite spaces both online and physically; strengthening relationships with key stakeholders; and engaging in advocacy trainings and direct advocacy in different global spaces. These are foundational structures and processes that strengthen movement-building and strategic advocacy in the long run, thus allowing grantees to capitalize on future advocacy opportunities.
